docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This data sheet serves to document the process of the light-sensing portion of Team BAMF's plant monitor.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
This light sensor unit is useful in determining the amount of light a plant recieves, and communicating that data with other sub-systems in a complete design.

This sensor uses a photoresistor to detect the amount of light as an impedance, and using an op-amp stage to amplify the signal to the proper voltage. This signal is then filtered for unwanted noise, and passed on to the next boards in the system.

For the complete design, refer to team report.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Block Diagram shows the lighting sensor of Team BAMF's plant monitor system. It uses a lighting sensor to determine whether or not the plant is recieving enough light, and then communicates with a teammate's board to move a shade to increase or decrease the light level.

The Block Diagram shows the critical wiring of components to the microcontroller, as well as the microcontroller peripherals, to document the necessary details of the system for communication and replication purposes.

docs.title: Sensor
docs.text:
Light Sensor

  1. PDV-P8103 through hole photoresistor

    • $0.72/each
    • PDV-P8103
    Pros Cons Low unit cost Moderate resistance range may provide less sensitivity in very dim conditions Documented rise and fall times for ease of calibration Its sensitivity only lists typical, making it hard to estimate variance (min and max) Resistance range of 16–33 kΩ at 10 lux is suitable for a voltage-divider circuit Slow response makes it unsuitable for tracking rapid light changes

  2. BPW34S-ND through hole photodiode

    • $2.11/each
    • BPW34S
    Pros Cons Fast response makes it suitable for detecting rapid changes in light Its output is current, requiring a resistor or transimpedance amplifier to produce a useful analog voltage Wide viewing angle helps capture light from different directions Near-infrared response means its output won't directly give plant-usable data without suitable filtering and calibration Detects visible light as well as near-infrared radiation, making it versatile for optical sensing Can be especially sensitive to placement

  3. QSD123 through hole phototransistor

    • $0.78/each
    • QSD123
    Pros Cons Transistor action amplifies the light-generated signal It is optimized for near-infrared light, not the visible spectrum used to assess typical plant lighting Its typical rise and fall times are around 7 μs, much faster than an LDR Doesn’t require amplifying circuit as per requirements Its narrow reception angle can help measure light from a specific direction Its output depends on the infrared spectrum, geometry, and circuit design so must be designed especially carefully

Choice: PDV-P8103 through hole photoresistor

Rationale: The PDV-P8103 is the best choice for our plant monitor because it is inexpensive, has a practical resistance range, and has documented response-time specifications. These characteristics allow us to detect changes in light intensity and compare the readings with thresholds based on the plant’s lighting requirements. Additionally, its variable resistance can be easily converted into an analog voltage using a simple voltage divider, allowing the sensor to interface directly with a microcontroller’s analog input. It is also the simplest to implement while following course guidelines.

docs.title: Amplification
docs.text:
Op Amp

  1. TLV272IP through hole Op Amp

    • $1.56/each
    • TLV272IP
    Pros Cons High 3 MHz bandwidth Higher power consumption than MCP6004 Wide 2.7–16 V supply range Input is not rail-to-rail Multiple channels in one IC Less channels than MCP6004-I/P

  2. MCP6004-I/P through hole Op Amp

    • $0.60/each
    • MCP6004-I/P
    Pros Cons Four channels in one IC Lower bandwidth (1 MHz) than TLV272IP and TL974IN Low power consumption (100 µA/channel) Limited to a 6 V maximum supply Rail-to-rail input and output; operates from 1.8–6 V Slower slew rate (0.6 V/µs) than the other two

  3. TL974IN through hole Op Amp

    • $1.66/each
    • TL974IN
    Pros Cons Highest bandwidth (12 MHz) Higher power consumption (2 mA/channel) Four channels in one IC Input is not rail-to-rail Low noise and rail-to-rail output Maximum supply is 12 V, lower than the TLV272IP's 16 V

Choice: MCP6004-I/P through hole Op Amp

Rationale: The MCP6004-I/P is the best choice because it provides four operational amplifiers in one package while consuming relatively little power. This is particularly important for our design because it allows us to amplify multiple sensor signals without needing several separate ICs. Its rail-to-rail input and output and compatibility with common 3.3 V and 5 V supplies also make it easier to interface with our embedded system. While it has a lower bandwidth than the TLV272IP and TL974IN, its 1 MHz bandwidth should be sufficient for our low-frequency sensor signals. Additionally, while all three options are compelling, the MCP6004-I/P is the cheapest and therefore more budget-friendly.

docs.title: Power Regulation
docs.text:
Voltage Regulators

  1. NJM7805FA through hole Linear Voltage Regulator

    • $1.85/each
    • NJM7805FA
    Pros Cons Fully insulated TO-220F package for electrical isolation Maximum operating temperature is 85°C Specified ripple rejection of 78 dB at 120 Hz allows for better stability Insulated package interferes with heatsink capabilities Over Temperature, Short Circuit protection More expensive than L7805ABV-DG

  2. L7805ABV-DG through hole Linear Voltage Regulator

    • $1.53/each
    • L7805ABV-DG
    Pros Cons Low cost compared with the MIC29151 Requires approximately 7 V or more input to maintain 5 V output under typical full-load conditions Supports input voltages up to 35 V Greater voltage drop creates more heat when the input voltage is much higher than 5 V Built-in thermal shutdown, current limiting, and safe-operating-area protection No enable pin for controlling the regulator through logic

  3. MIC29151-5.0WT through hole Linear Voltage Regulator

    • $4.96/each
    • MIC29151-5.0WT
    Pros Cons Low dropout voltage (600 mV maximum at 1.5 A) allows operation with an input closer to 5 V More expensive than traditional 7805 regulators Built-in reverse-polarity, overcurrent, and overtemperature protection improve circuit safety Five-pin package requires more connections than a standard three-pin regulator Enable pin allows the microcontroller or other logic to turn the regulator on and off Maximum input voltage is 26 V, lower than the 35 V rating of the other two options

Choice: L7805ABV-DG through hole Linear Voltage Regulator

Rationale: The L7805ABV-DG is the best choice because it provides a reliable 5 V output at a low cost and includes built-in thermal shutdown and current limiting. This is particularly important for our plant monitor because it needs a stable power supply for the microcontroller and sensor circuits without adding unnecessary cost or complexity. Although the NJM7805FA offers similar protection features, it is more expensive and does not provide a significant advantage for our design. The MIC29151-5.0WT has a lower dropout voltage and an enable pin, but these features are not essential if our wall adapter provides sufficient input voltage. Therefore, it offers the best balance of cost, simplicity, and performance for our project.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Power Sources

  1. YS39-2402500-D1J AC to DC Wall Adapter

    • $15.20/each
    • NGE30U12-P1J
    Pros Cons Provides stable, regulated power for continuous monitoring Requires a nearby AC outlet and limits portability Can supply up to 30 W Costs more initially than the battery holder Includes overload, overvoltage, and short-circuit protection Its 12 V output must be stepped down, adding a regulator and associated circuitry

  2. KXOB25-12X1F-TR Solar Cell

    • $3.14/each
    • KXOB25-12X1F-TR
    Pros Cons Uses renewable energy Maximum output is only 24.5 mW, requiring many cells Very small and lightweight Its 0.56 V operating voltage requires boost circuitry Suitable for an outdoor monitor exposed to sunlight Reliable overnight operation requires additional energy storage

  3. 36-2477-ND Battery Holder and E91VP AA Batteries

    • $1.99/each - Battery Holder

    • 36-2477-ND

    • $0.42/each (at 620 pcs; consistent with retail) - AA Batteries

    • E91VP
    Pros Cons Inexpensive holder at $1.99 Batteries must be purchased separately and eventually replaced Mounts directly to the PCB using through-hole pins Cells provide only about 1.5V each, lower margin to 5V requirement Batteries are replaceable, so the monitor can operate without a wall outlet Battery voltage declines with discharge, and runtime depends on battery capacity and system current

Choice: MEAN WELL NGE30U12-P1J wall adapter

Rationale: The MEAN WELL NGE30U12-P1J wall adapter is the best choice for our plant monitor because it provides a stable, regulated 12 V DC supply with sufficient current capacity to power the microcontroller, light sensor, and other system components. This is particularly important because the monitor needs consistent power to collect light measurements and compare them against thresholds based on the plant's lighting requirements. Unlike battery-powered alternatives, the wall adapter does not require periodic battery replacement or recharging, making it reliable for continuous indoor operation. It also requires much simpler circuitry compared to the solar cells to connect to the PCB, as well as less components.

This Bill of Materials documents Team BAMF's light sensor module, with all the necessary parts (with suppliers and datasheets) per prototype unit. This serves as documentation to the necessary parts that make up the subsystem, so it can be referred to and replicated.

Some important notes: The unit quantity is how many of the component in the individual module, the unit cost is how much each individual component costs, and the total prototype cost is how much a it would cost to complete a prototype with the parts. # Ordered is extra parts for breadbaording and replacements if need be, not how many are necessary.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is designed to support Team BAMF's Plant Monitor system by introducing a light sensing circuit to sense the ambient light around the plant and compare it to the necessary light, sending signals to a motor connected to a shade to increase or decrease light amount (depending on what's necessary), and data to a screen letting users know what status the plant's lighting is in (good/bad).

It does so by using a photoresistor to detect light as an impedance, which then is amplified by an op-amp to generate a complete signal as a voltage. This voltage is communicated to the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano micrcontroller for ADC to DAC processing, finally being sent as an analog signal to the motor on another board and UART data to the screen on another board. The whole system is powered by a wall adapter connected to a barrel jack, regualted by a linear voltage regulator outputing 5V.

Figure 3: Team BAMF Light Sensor schematic.

NOTE: Every resistor is rated for 1/4 W, every capacitor is rated for 50 V, and the fuse is rated for 2.5 A. Power budget can be found here

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A power budget is necessary to ensure that the power source and voltage regulators can provide enough power for every component in the system. It helps prevent power shortages, voltage drops, and overloaded components while ensuring the system operates reliably. It also helps determine the appropriate power supply and estimate battery life if the system is battery-powered.

First, all major components and their maximum current requirements were identified using their datasheets. Next, the components were assigned to appropriate voltage rails, and their current requirements were totaled with an additional 25% safety margin. Then, suitable voltage regulators and an external power source were selected to meet the system's power requirements. Finally, the available current was checked to ensure the power source could support all components.

Figure 4: Team BAMF Light Sensor Power Budget

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: From the prepare Power Budget, the L7805ABV-DG voltage regulator is rated for up to 1.5 A, leaving approximately 757.04 mA of available current capacity on the rail. The selected 12V wall supply can provide up to 2.5 A, while the regulator is listed as drawing 1.5 A, leaving 1 A of remaining current capacity at the source. Overall, the listed current ratings suggest that the system has sufficient current capacity to operate, even with the safety margin. Additionally, the fuse was selected to be 2.5A based on the maximum amperage that can be supplied by the power supply for expandability purposes.
